raw_text:
### Introduction
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a progressive infiltrative cardiomyopathy characterized by the extracellular deposition of misfolded amyloid fibrils in the myocardial interstitium. Traditionally viewed as a rare and rapidly fatal disease, CA is now increasingly recognized as an underdiagnosed cause of heart failure [1,2]. Recent breakthroughs in multi-modality non-invasive imaging, diagnostic algorithms, and highly effective disease-modifying therapies have revolutionized the clinical management of CA [3,4]. The two principal forms of systemic amyloidosis that commonly result in clinically significant cardiac involvement are immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloidosis and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis [5].

### Pathophysiology and Subtypes
The pathophysiology of CA varies according to the precursor protein. AL amyloidosis is caused by a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia or B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder that secretes unstable monoclonal light chains. These proteins misfold and self-assemble into insoluble fibrils, causing both structural disruption and direct local oxidative stress and cellular toxicity to the myocardium [6,7]. AL amyloidosis runs a highly aggressive clinical course with poor outcomes if untreated [8]. 

Conversely, ATTR amyloidosis stems from the hepatic protein transthyretin, a tetramer responsible for transporting thyroxine and retinol [9]. ATTR is categorized into two forms: wild-type (ATTRwt)—typically presenting in older individuals, predominantly males, and characterized by the age-related instability of the wild-type protein [10,11]—and hereditary (ATTRm), which is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the transthyretin (*TTR*) gene, leading to accelerated protein dissociation [9,12]. 

### Clinical Presentation and Red Flags
Early recognition of clinical "red flags" is essential to avoid diagnostic delays [13]. Patients with CA frequently present with progressive symptoms of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), such as exertional dyspnea, fatigue, and lower-extremity edema [14]. Extracardiac manifestations provide important clues: bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, and spontaneous biceps tendon rupture often precede cardiac symptoms by years in ATTRwt [14,15]. 

Electrocardiographic findings of low QRS voltage, mismatched with marked left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy on echocardiography, are highly suggestive but occur in only a minority of patients, while a pseudo-infarct pattern in precordial leads is more common [15]. Echocardiography typically reveals concentric ventricular wall thickening, a granular "sparkling" myocardial appearance, interatrial septal thickening, and moderate-to-severe diastolic dysfunction [15]. Crucially, speckle-tracking echocardiography demonstrates a classic "apical sparing" pattern of longitudinal strain, which holds high diagnostic specificity for CA [15].

### The Diagnostic Paradigm Shift
The diagnostic paradigm has shifted away from mandatory endomyocardial biopsy [1]. A validated non-invasive diagnostic algorithm now permits a definitive diagnosis of ATTR-CA under specific clinical criteria [16]. Bone-avid scintigraphy using technetium-99m labeled pyrophosphate ($^{99\text{m}}\text{Tc-PYP}$), 3,3-diphosphono-1,2-propanodicarboxylic acid ($^{99\text{m}}\text{Tc-DPD}$), or hydroxymethylene diphosphonate ($^{99\text{m}}\text{Tc-HMDP}$) demonstrates high sensitivity and specificity for ATTR-CA in the absence of a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia [16,17]. 

Because low-grade bone-scintigraphy uptake can occasionally occur in AL amyloidosis, simultaneous screening with serum/urine immunofixation electrophoresis and serum free light chain (FLC) assays is mandatory to rule out clonal dyscrasias [18]. If a monoclonal protein is detected, histological confirmation via tissue biopsy (fat pad, salivary gland, or endomyocardial) with Congo red staining and mass spectrometry remains mandatory to differentiate AL from ATTR amyloidosis [3,4,16]. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is another critical tool, revealing diffuse subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and increased native T1 and extracellular volume (ECV) values, which correlate with the burden of amyloid deposition and long-term prognosis [19,20].

### Therapeutic Landscape
Treatment strategies diverge sharply based on the underlying subtype. The management of AL amyloidosis focuses on rapidly eradicating the clone. The combination of daratumumab (an anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody) with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone (CyBorD) has recently become the standard of care based on the ANDROMEDA trial, yielding rapid, deep, and durable hematologic responses [21,22].

For ATTR amyloidosis, the landmark ATTR-ACT trial established tafamidis, a kinetic stabilizer that binds to the TTR tetramer and prevents its dissociation into amyloidogenic monomers, as a foundational therapy [23]. Tafamidis significantly reduces all-cause mortality, cardiovascular hospitalizations, and the rate of functional decline in both ATTRwt and ATTRm patients [23,28]. Other therapeutic strategies employ gene-silencing technologies. RNA interference (RNAi) agents like patisiran and vutrisiran, along with the antisense oligonucleotide inotersen, inhibit the hepatic translation of TTR, showing substantial benefit in polyneuropathy and promising results in stabilizing cardiac function [24,25,26,27]. Registries such as the Transthyretin Amyloidosis Outcomes Survey (THAOS) continue to clarify disease patterns [29]. Finally, innovative therapies such as CRISPR-Cas9 in vivo gene editing are under investigation to offer a durable, single-dose solution by permanently knocking down hepatic TTR production [30].

### Conclusion
Cardiac amyloidosis has transitioned from a rare, untreatable condition to a highly manageable disease. Early multi-disciplinary diagnosis, facilitated by non-invasive imaging, and timely initiation of targeted agents are essential to improve long-term prognosis.
